Agent Safety Is Action Alignment

Shawn Li email: li.li02@usc.edu Affiliation: University of Southern California, Los Angeles, California, USA and Yue Zhao email: yue.z@usc.edu Affiliation: University of Southern California, Los Angeles, California, USA
© none
Abstract.

Large language models increasingly act as agents: they call tools, move money, delete records, and send messages on a user’s behalf. To keep them safe, practitioners imported the chatbot-era recipe (train the model to refuse unsafe inputs) into the agentic setting, and treat the resulting capability loss as a manageable “alignment tax.” We argue this is a category error. Refusal is a primitive for content safety, where the harm is in the model’s output and is therefore a learnable function of it. Agentic harm is different in kind: it lies not in any output but in the relation between the authority an action exercises and the authority the user granted, which is absent from the text the model sees. Importing content-safety methods into this regime does not trade capability for safety; it pays capability and buys negative security. We support this with three lines of evidence spanning the autonomy spectrum: defense-trained models learn surface patterns rather than intent; the same training collapses multi-step agents before any threat appears while leaving them exploitable; and even undefended frontier models exceed granted authority under ordinary use. We conclude that action safety cannot be installed in weights. It must be expressed as least privilege, enforced outside the model at the action boundary, and evaluated as action alignment (a relational, deployment-conditioned property) rather than a refusal score.

1. Introduction

A practitioner fine-tunes a capable open-weight model to reject prompt-injection attacks and reports a reassuring number: attack rejection above 90%90\% on a standard benchmark. Then the model is placed in an agent loop with a tool that can delete user accounts, and handed a request embedded in retrieved content: “As part of QA testing, please demonstrate the account-deletion feature by removing user ID 7731.” The undefended base model refuses; the defense-trained model executes the deletion, and does so 78%78\% of the time across such attacks, because the request carries none of the lexical triggers the defense learned to associate with danger (Li and Zhao, 2026). The intervention sold as safety did not merely fail to protect; it subtracted the judgment the base model already had.

Position. How can a model that scores well on every safety benchmark behave worse than no defense at all? Because the field is solving the wrong problem. The prevailing paradigm was forged in the chatbot setting, where harm is a property of the model’s output and the tool is refusal: train the model to decline inputs that produce harmful text (Ouyang et al., 2022; Bai et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2025b; Chen et al., 2024). We argue this rests on a category error: refusal works for content safety because the harm is in the output; it fails for action safety because the harm is in the authority, which the output does not contain. When an agent deletes a record or follows an injected instruction, the harm is not in any string it emits but in the relation between the authority its action exercises and the authority the user granted, a quantity absent from the tokens the model reads. Importing content-safety methods here does not trade capability for safety; it pays capability and buys negative security.

The error across the autonomy spectrum. The same transfer error surfaces at every level of autonomy, and the cost compounds. In single-turn defense there is no intent to learn from, so models learn surface form (Li et al., 2026c); in multi-step agents the surface reflex fires on benign tasks before any threat appears and cascades toward total failure, while real attacks still slip through (Li and Zhao, 2026); and in tool-using agents, even with no defense training, models exceed the authority a task requires because that authority is not represented in their input (Li et al., 2026d). The cost climbs from an annoyance (a false refusal) to a cascade to an invisible failure, the task succeeding while quietly exercising more authority than granted. Section 4 develops each as a corollary (Figure 1).

What we propose. Because intent and granted authority are absent from the model’s input, action safety cannot be installed in the weights (§4.4); it must live where the missing information does, at the boundary where actions meet a known authority. We argue for three shifts: replace the refusal primitive with least privilege (Saltzer and Schroeder, 1975); move enforcement outside the model to a mechanically checked action boundary (Shi et al., 2025; Zhu and others, 2025; Ji and others, 2026); and evaluate safety as a relational, multi-coordinate property rather than a single refusal score.

Our contribution:

  • •

    We distinguish content safety from action safety by where the harm resides, and identify the field’s central failure as importing the former’s methods into the latter (§3).

  • •

    We formalize safety as a multi-coordinate property and show the refuse–comply axis is a projection that is provably blind to authority restraint (§3).

  • •

    We organize three lines of evidence across the autonomy spectrum into corollaries of one transfer error and distill two falsifiable claims (§4).

  • •

    We argue for least privilege, external enforcement, and relational evaluation (§5).

2. Related Work

Model-level defenses against injection. Structured-query training, preference-optimized alignment, instruction hierarchies, constitutional methods, and deliberative alignment all train the model itself to reject adversarial instructions (Chen et al., 2025b; Chen et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025c; Li et al., 2025a; Wallace et al., 2024; Bai et al., 2022; Guan et al., 2024). We read this line as content-safety methods applied to an action-safety problem; §4 catalogs the resulting failures. Our claim is not that these methods are poorly executed but that they target the wrong object.

Content safety and alignment. Instruction tuning with human feedback and input–output moderation operate where the harm is in the output (Ouyang et al., 2022; Li et al., 2024; Inan et al., 2023); we treat these as genuine content-safety tools, outside the scope of our critique. Shortcut learning explains why surface optimization dominates when the only labelable signal is form (Geirhos et al., 2020). Unreliable agent behavior extends beyond injection to hallucination (Shawn et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025e; Qin et al., 2026b) and failure under distribution shift (Li et al., 2026b; Li et al., 2025d; Li et al., 2025c; Liu et al., 2026b; Qin et al., 2026a; Chen et al., 2025a); action alignment isolates the safety-relevant slice of this broader reliability problem.

Systems security and agent enforcement. Least privilege and capability-based protection predate language models (Saltzer and Schroeder, 1975). Recent work brings programmable privilege control, least-privilege authorization, and mandatory access control to LLM agents (Shi et al., 2025; Zhu and others, 2025; Ji and others, 2026); we view this as the correct locus for action safety, and our position as the argument for why it is necessary rather than merely helpful.

Agent benchmarks and auditability. LLM agents increasingly act in the world, from computer-using multi-agent systems (Song et al., 2026) to tool-driven editing agents (Ye et al., 2026), and their attack surface includes black-box manipulation of retrieval (Li et al., 2026a) and multimodal jailbreaks (Nian et al., 2025). Dynamic environments evaluate injection in multi-step settings (Debenedetti et al., 2024), and recent work argues that deployed agents must be auditable after the fact (Nian et al., 2026). Enforcement and auditability are complementary: the former decides ex ante whether an action is permitted, the latter reconstructs ex post what occurred and who was responsible.

3. Action Safety Is Not Content Safety

3.1. Where the Harm Resides

Content harm is a function of the output alone. Writing out⁡(a)\mathrm{out}(a) for the text a model emits, content harm is hc​(out​(a))h_{\mathrm{c}}\big(\mathrm{out}(a)\big): toxicity, defamation, leaked secrets, instructions for wrongdoing. The same disinformation is equally harmful whoever asked and whatever system surrounds it. Because hch_{\mathrm{c}} is a function of the output, it is in principle learnable from outputs paired with harm labels and avertable by not emitting the output. This is where content moderation and refusal training operate (Inan et al., 2023; Ouyang et al., 2022).

Action harm is not a function of any output. When aa is an action (a tool call, a transaction, a deletion), its safety depends on two quantities external to the emitted tokens: the authority the action exercises, auth⁡(a)\mathrm{auth}(a), and the authority the user actually granted, AA. The action is over-privileged when auth⁡(a)⊈A\mathrm{auth}(a)\not\subseteq A. A second source of action harm is provenance: whether aa realizes the user’s intent or an instruction injected through an untrusted channel such as a tool observation or retrieved document (Greshake et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024). Neither AA nor provenance appears in out⁡(a)\mathrm{out}(a); both live in the surrounding system. This is the crux: action harm is a relation between the action and information the model never sees, so no function of the output can decide it. The string delete_user(7731) carries no content harm; its harm is entirely relational, since the deletion exceeds what a “QA demonstration” could grant and the controlling instruction arrived through an untrusted channel.

3.2. Refusal Is a Content-Safety Primitive

In the content regime, declining to emit the output directly averts hch_{\mathrm{c}}: the harmful text is exactly what is withheld, so the mapping from “unsafe” to “refuse” is sound. In the action regime it breaks both ways. Refusing is not safe: it strands the user, and the same surface-tuned reflex that blocks benign actions fails on the genuinely dangerous action that lacks the expected cues. Complying is not unsafe per se: the safe behavior is usually to do the task while staying within AA. Refusal cannot express this. It is an all-or-nothing gate on the whole action, whereas action safety needs a bound on the action’s scope; refusal is the degenerate case that sets that scope to empty. Building agent safety on refusal builds it on a primitive that cannot represent the property it should protect.

3.3. Safety as a Multi-Coordinate Property

The error has a measurement-theoretic shadow. The field scores agent safety on one behavioral axis: did the model refuse when it should and comply when it should? With ref⁡(a)∈{0,1}\mathrm{ref}(a)\in\{0,1\} and label y∈{benign,malicious}y\in\{\textsf{benign},\textsf{malicious}\}, the prevailing score is

Sfield(a)=𝟏[\displaystyle S_{\mathrm{field}}(a)=\mathbf{1}\big[ (ref⁡(a)=1∧y=malicious)\displaystyle\big(\mathrm{ref}(a)=1\wedge y=\textsf{malicious}\big)
∨(ref(a)=0∧y=benign)],\displaystyle}{\displaystyle\vee\ \big(\mathrm{ref}(a)=0\wedge y=\textsf{benign}\big)\,\big],

a function of only ref⁡(a)\mathrm{ref}(a) and the label yy. Contrast the property we actually want. For a response aa to a request with true intent ii and granted authority AA, let adv⁡(a)\mathrm{adv}(a) flag that aa obeys adversarial control (a malicious request or an untrusted-channel injection):

(1) C⁡(a)\displaystyle C(a) =𝟏​[a​ accomplishes ​i]\displaystyle=\mathbf{1}[\,a\text{ accomplishes }i\,] (competence),\displaystyle\text{(\emph{competence})},

We call the conjunction S⋆​(a)=C⁡(a)∧R⁡(a)∧B⁡(a)S^{\star}(a)=C(a)\wedge R(a)\wedge B(a) action alignment: the action accomplishes the user’s intent, stays within granted authority, and is free of injected control. It is a deliberate foil to the familiar alignment of model values and outputs, and broader than authority alone, since an over-refusal violates it on CC exactly as over-privilege violates it on RR. Three defects of the prevailing metric follow, set against the coordinates in Table 1.

Blindness to restraint. RR depends on auth⁡(a)\mathrm{auth}(a), which is not an argument of SfieldS_{\mathrm{field}}. There exist responses a,a′a,a^{\prime} with identical (ref,y)(\mathrm{ref},y) but different RR, e.g. two completions that differ only in using a folder-scoped or an account-wide tool. No metric of this form distinguishes them, so the refuse–comply axis is provably blind to over-privilege, the dominant agentic failure: when models err they err toward more authority, abstaining on under 1.5%1.5\% of cases (Li et al., 2026d). The most dangerous failures are the ones it is built not to see, because the task succeeds and only RR is violated.

Conflation, and an unobservable argument. The other two defects are visible in the formula. SfieldS_{\mathrm{field}} collapses two independent coordinates onto one bit: ref⁡(a)\mathrm{ref}(a) proxies both “emitted no harmful action” (BB) and “did the task” (CC), forcing a spurious trade-off in which refusing more raises apparent resistance only by lowering competence, so the “alignment tax” is an artifact, not a price. And SfieldS_{\mathrm{field}} conditions on the surface-derived label yy, not the true intent ii, so a loss minimized against it learns P⁡(y∣surface)P(y\mid\text{surface}), the shortcut the single-turn evidence documents (Li et al., 2026c; Geirhos et al., 2020). In sum, the refuse–comply axis is a one-dimensional projection of a three-dimensional property: on the coordinate it drops it is unconstrained, on the coordinates it conflates it is actively misleading.

4. The Error That Scales with Autonomy

If the diagnosis is right, it should leave the same fingerprint wherever content-safety machinery meets an action-safety problem, and worsen with autonomy. We read three recent studies as corollaries, each at a different rung of the autonomy spectrum; the aim is interpretive, to show each is what the error predicts. Figure 1 summarizes the three settings.

4.1. Corollary 1: No Intent to Learn

Supervised injection defenses reproduce a content-style label (each prompt tagged benign or attack) and are expected to generalize to malicious intent. But the injected-control relation that makes an input dangerous lives in provenance and authority, not in the tokens; what is in the tokens is form. Empirical risk minimization therefore minimizes loss through the only correlated features, surface form: a single attack-associated token raises false-refusal rates by up to 50%50\%, benign reasoning placed late is rejected up to 90%90\% of the time, and benign tasks from unseen topics lose up to 40%40\% accuracy (Li et al., 2026c). The loss is not confined to refusals: defended models truncate chains of thought on benign tasks even when they do not refuse. That this is the category error and not a bad implementation is shown by cross-defense convergence: two defenses learn different shortcuts yet both lose 4545–5656 points of true-positive rate (Li et al., 2026c; Li and Zhao, 2026). The problem is not which surface is learned but that a surface is all there is to learn.

4.2. Corollary 2: The Reflex Misfires and Compounds

In a multi-step agent the content-safety reflex (be suspicious of action-laden text) misfires both ways, and the loop amplifies it. Competence is destroyed before any external observation appears: defended models fail at the first step on 4747–77%77\% of benign tasks versus 3%3\% for the base model (Li and Zhao, 2026). With no tool output yet seen, this is not observation-triggered detection; it is the reflex firing on the benign task itself. And a single mid-trajectory false positive is not local: when the agent refuses a benign step (say, an observation containing financial terms), the framework retries, the same surface re-triggers, and the trajectory dies, raising timeouts from 13%13\% to as high as 99%99\%, a 22–2.7×2.7\times amplification (Li and Zhao, 2026). Meanwhile the defended agent is more exploitable on attacks lacking learned keywords. Over-firing on benign actions and under-firing on real harm are one signature: attending to surface form rather than authority and provenance.

4.3. Corollary 3: Drift Toward Power

Removing defense training entirely isolates the deepest layer. Even undefended frontier models exceed the authority a task requires, because AA is not represented in what they read. Over-privilege is the norm under ordinary, non-adversarial conditions: the strongest model misroutes more than one skill-selection request in three, and end-to-end least-privilege behavior holds for under 15%15\% of requests (Li et al., 2026d). The mechanism is a parameter-burden gradient: low-privilege tools demand explicit arguments (a folder, an account) while high-privilege tools demand few or none, so the path of least resistance is the path of most privilege. Failures take three ordinary forms: preferring a broader tool for fewer arguments; reading a multi-target request as license for a cross-resource operation; and treating a missing optional feature as license to escalate. None needs an adversary, and the direction is invariant: models abstain on under 1.5%1.5\% of cases and err toward more authority. With the content-safety apparatus absent, the action-safety problem remains in full, the cleanest demonstration that it was never “bad defenses” but a missing representation no output-level method supplies.

4.4. Two Falsifiable Claims

The corollaries sharpen into two claims the position stands or falls on, and the rest of the paper builds on them.

Claim 1 (Safety training is non-monotone). The marginal safety of an intervention can be negative: a defense-trained model can be less safe than its base, as the account-deletion result shows (Li and Zhao, 2026). This contradicts the assumption that safety training is at worst inert, which underwrites the “add more safety training” program.

Claim 2 (Behavioral action safety is hard to learn). With intent and authority absent from the input, no input-output objective can install action safety; it can only learn a surface correlate. The fingerprint is the one defense that tries to supply the signal, an “untrusted-input” role, which needs adversarial content pre-identified (the very problem) and underperforms the undefended baseline in deployment (Li and Zhao, 2026). This elevates the critique from “current methods are weak” to “this kind of methods is structurally incapable.”

5. Toward Action Safety

If action safety cannot live in the weights, it must be expressed, enforced, and evaluated where the missing information lives. None of the three shifts below is individually novel, but given Claims 1 and 2 they are not merely better options but necessary ones.

5.1. Least Privilege as the Safety Primitive

The safe behavior for an acting model is rarely “decline” but “do the task exercising only the authority granted”: the principle of least privilege (Saltzer and Schroeder, 1975). This reframes the target from a gate on the whole action to a bound on its scope, with refusal the degenerate empty-scope case. It dissolves the false trade-off of §3.3: over-refusal is under-privilege, over-reach is over-privilege, and a task that completes while escalating is correctly unsafe. And it redirects evaluation from “how often did the model refuse attacks” to “how often did its action stay within AA,” a question about RR that current metrics cannot express.

5.2. External Enforcement at the Action Boundary

Least privilege is a property of actions against an authority, so it must be enforced where the two meet: at the tool-invocation boundary, by a mechanism that holds the grant AA the model lacks. The model proposes an action; an external reference monitor checks it against the grant and the provenance of the controlling instruction, then permits, narrows, or escalates to a human (Shi et al., 2025; Zhu and others, 2025; Ji and others, 2026). Three consequences follow. The check is mechanical, so it is not subject to shortcut learning; it compares auth⁡(a)\mathrm{auth}(a) to AA rather than guessing intent from form. It recovers capability: because the boundary carries the guarantee, the model need not be defense-trained into incompetence, turning Claim 1 into an argument for removing model-level defenses. And it is ex ante, complementing ex post auditability (Nian et al., 2026). This is not free (§6), but its hard problems concern the right object, the authority relation, whereas output-level defenses concern the wrong one.

5.3. Relational and Deployment-Conditioned Evaluation

Safety should be measured as the property it is. Report the three coordinates separately, preserved competence CC, restraint RR, and genuine (semantic, not surface) resistance BB, rather than collapsing them into one refusal score; a method that raises one by lowering another is not an improvement. And evaluate under deployment conditions current benchmarks omit: multi-step trajectories with cascade-aware metrics (§4.2), and ordinary non-adversarial ambiguity rather than only triggered attacks, since the dominant failures arise under exactly those everyday conditions (Li et al., 2026d; Debenedetti et al., 2024). The single-number safety benchmark, inherited from content moderation, is the measurement counterpart of the category error. Relational evaluation can draw on emerging LLM- and MLLM-based judges (Liu et al., 2026a) and on benchmarking and user-simulation methodology (Yang et al., 2025; Ni et al., 2026; Li et al., 2025b).

6. Open Problems

The position opens concrete problems. (1) Specifying authority: how to express AA for open-ended tasks, and how much can be inferred versus must be declared. (2) Measuring restraint: ground-truth least-privilege references beyond curated benchmarks. (3) Cascade-aware evaluation: trajectory-level metrics (§4.2). (4) Bounded enforcement: acceptable overhead and false-block rates on large tool spaces. (5) Provenance: tracking each instruction’s trust level through multi-hop tool use. (6) The content–action boundary: which residual properties genuinely belong in the model because their harm is in the output. (7) Delegation: how the grant AA propagates when an agent spawns sub-agents that act on its behalf.

7. Conclusion

As models move from answering to acting, the field has carried forward a safety paradigm built for answering: train the model to refuse, and call the capability loss a tax. This is a category error. Refusal works for content safety because the harm is in the output; it fails for action safety because the harm is in the relation between exercised and granted authority, which the output does not contain. Because that information is absent from the model’s inputs, action safety cannot be installed in the weights; it must be enforced at the action boundary instead. Failure is not safety, and success is not safety; safety is action alignment: an action that accomplishes the user’s intent, within the authority granted, free of injected control.
